title: Enterprise-Ready MCP: Security Patterns and the "4-Legged" Identity Challenge - Paulina Xu

segments.text: Hi everybody, thanks for being here. I'm
Paulina, the CEO of Aentic Fabric and
today I'm going to talk about what it
actually takes to make MCP enterprise
ready and specifically why security and
identity are becoming the defining
problems when you move beyond local
development. So a framing I'm going to
use throughout this talk is what I call
the four-legged identity challenge. But
one thing that I want to make clear
right off the bat is that four legs is
actually just the minimum viable
complexity. In real world agentic
systems, you often end up with five,
six, or even longer chains of
delegation. And the complexity grows
very quickly. And the systems that we're
used to, such as OOTH, were never
designed for that. So what I want to do
today is to walk through how we got
here, why the traditional models break,
and what the failure modes look like in
practice and then how we can actually
build systems that are safe to deploy in
production.
Okay, so let's rewind a bit and start
with how OOTH was originally designed
before agents were even a part of the
picture. So on this slide, what you're
looking at is the canonical OOTH model.
There have three actors, the user, the
application and the IDP. So the user
initiates a request, the application
redirects them to the identity provider.
They authenticate, grant consent and the
application receives an access token. So
at this point, the system has a very
clear and well- definfined identity
model. The token represents the user.
the application is acting on behalf of
that user and every request made with
that token is traceable back to this
specific user and this specific consent
event. And what's important here is not
just that the delegation works, but that
the delegation is simple and explicit.
There is exactly one hop. The user
authorizes the application and that it's
that's it. So there's no ambiguity about
who is acting, no intermediate reasoning
layer and no transformation of identity
across multiple systems. The entity that
holds the token is the exact same entity
that then goes and makes a request. And
that simplicity is exactly why OOTH
works so well in traditional web
architecture.
So now let's extend this model slightly.
So on this slide you can see that we've
added a downstream API. So now the flow
becomes user to application to API. The
application takes the access token that
it received from the IDP and uses that
to call the API. The API validates the
token, check scopes and enforces
authorization. This is still fully
within the design assumptions of OOTH.
Even though the system is now
distributed across multiple services,
the identity model remains intact. The
API can still see user identity through
the token and it can still enforce
permissions correctly and the delegation
chain here is still short and explicit.
So this is what we call the three-legged
OOTH flow and it has a very important
property which is that the application
is still the final executor of the
user's intent. There is no autonomous
system in between. There's no dynamic
decision-making layer. The application
is deterministic. It knows exactly which
API it's calling and why. So even as
systems became more complex, OOTH still
scaled well because the core assumption
still held. The entity acting is the
entity that was authorized.
So now is where things are starting to
change. Up until now, everything we've
looked at assumes that the application
is the one making the decisions and
executing the actions. But once we
introduce agents, that assumption no
longer holds. So on this slide we add
two new components into this system an
agent and an MCP server. So now the flow
becomes user to agent to MCP to API. And
this is the exact point where the OOTH
model starts to break because now the
application is no longer the final
executor of the user's intent. Instead
it hands off its control to an agent.
The agent then decides which tools to
call, when to call them, and how to
structure those calls. The MCP server
then executes those tool invocations
often against downstream APIs. So the
execution path has changed from a single
explicit delegation to multihop dynamic
delegation chain. And this introduces a
very fundamental ambiguity which is that
when the MCP server is now calling the
API, whose identity is actually being
used? Is it the user who originally
initiated the request? Is it the agent
who made the decision or is it the MCP
server who is actually executing the
call? OOTH doesn't have a very clear
answer for this because it assumes that
tokens are used by the same entity that
they were issued to and that they are
scoped to a specific audience and this
creates two immediate problems. The
first one is that tokens are
audiencebound. A token issued for one
service cannot simply be reused for
another. So the token that the
application received is not
automatically valid for the MCP server
or the downstream API.
The second issue is that identity easily
gets lost along this chain. If the MCP
server uses its own credentials to call
the API, then from the API's
perspective, the calls coming from the
MCP server, not the original user. So
that effectively means that the original
user's context has disappeared. And this
is what we call identity loss midchain.
And it's the core of the four-legged
identity challenge. And more
importantly, this isn't just a
theoretical issue. This is what is
actually leading to production failures
such as overp permission actions, data
leakage, and a lack of auditability. All
of these stem from the system no longer
knowing who is actually acting.
And more importantly, this doesn't just
stop at four legs. As shown here, once
you introduce federation, multiple IDPS,
agentto agent communication, this chain
becomes significantly more complex. You
might have one agent that calls another
agent, multiple MCP servers, different
identity providers per service. So now
identity is not just being passed along
a chain, it's being transformed across a
graph of systems. So for example,
imagine an enterprise workflow where the
agent pulls data from Salesforce,
enriches it with its internal analytics
and then sends messages via Slack. Each
of those systems has its own identity
model. Each may require different
scopes, different tokens, and even
different identity providers. So now the
problem is no longer just how do we pass
identity forward. It becomes how do we
preserve identity coherently across
heterogeneous systems over multiple hops
potentially across time and that is
where traditional ooth falls short.
So what are some actual patterns that
people are using today? This slide helps
to lay out four common approaches but
each one has its own trade-off. The
first one is non-delegating client
credentials. This is perhaps the
simplest model. The MCP server calls
downstream APIs as itself. It's very
easy to implement. It's widely supported
and it works everywhere, but it
completely loses user identity.
Downstream systems have no idea who
originally initiated that action. So the
second method is token exchange. This is
the cleanest model conceptually. You
take a user scope token and you exchange
it for a new token that is valid for the
downstream API. So this preserves
identity end to end. But the issue is
that support for RFC8693
is still extremely limited. The third
method is pre-injected tokens. So this
is where the application fetches all the
tokens it needs up front and passes them
through the system. This works with any
IDP, but it assumes that you know every
single downstream dependency and every
single downstream call that you need to
make ahead of time, which doesn't align
well with the dynamic nature of agents.
And the last one is outofband login.
This is where the user has to explicitly
authorize every single downstream
service. This is very secure but it
introduces friction and coordination
complexity. So already you can see that
solving identity in these systems isn't
just a protocol problem. It's a systems
design problem.
So let's go a little bit deeper into
token exchange because this is really
the core primitive. So on this slide,
you can see what an actual token
exchange request looks like. You take a
subject token, which is typically the
user's access token, and you request for
a new token with a different audience.
That new token represents a delegated
identity. It still encodes for the user,
but it's scoped specifically for a
downstream resource. This is critical
because it allows you to preserve
identity while still respecting the
audience constraints of OOTH. But the
reality today unfortunately is that
support for this is still very uneven.
For example, Keycloak supports this very
well. Microsoft Entra doesn't support it
and Octa only supports it partially
through claims. So in practice, many
systems tend to introduce a broker layer
that handles token exchange centrally.
So at this point, a natural question
that arises is if OOTH is not enough for
Agentic systems, then what helps to fill
in the missing pieces? So that's exactly
what this slide shows. These four RFC's
work together to make OOTH usable in a
world where agents are discovering
systems dynamically, registering
themselves, and then carrying identity
across multiple hops. And the easiest
way to understand these four is to treat
them as a series of questions that your
agent needs answered along along a
system. So the first one is RFC 9728,
which is resource metadata. So this
answers the question, I'm an agent and I
just found a protected resource on an
MCP server. What is it and what kind of
O setup does it expect me to use? So in
plain terms, this is just the resource
introducing itself. It tells the client
which authorization servers it trusts
and what scopes or access patterns may
be relevant. That matters because in a
dynamic environment, an agent cannot
assume ahead of time which IDP or O
server an MCP server belongs to.
So RFC 9728 is really the starting point
for discovery. Before the agent can
actually ask for a token, it first needs
to learn where that trust starts. So now
once the agent has that information, the
next step is RFC8414,
which is authorization server metadata.
So this helps to answer the question,
now that I know which authorization
server I'm supposed to use, how do I
actually talk to it? So the
authorization server publishes a
metadata document that tells the client
certain things like where the
authorization endpoint is, where the
token endpoint is, where to fetch
signing keys, and what capabilities are
supported. I usually describe RFC 8414
as essentially the authorization servers
instruction manual. So while RFC 9728
tells you which O system matters,
RFC8414
tells you how that O system works. And
so after that comes RFC7591
which is dynamic client registration. So
this answers the question question if
I'm a new agent and I don't already have
an identity in this authorization server
how do I then become a recognized
client. In traditional OOTH this is done
manually. A human has to come in and
create a client in the admin portal
copies a client ID maybe provisions a
secret and then wires everything up in
advance. But agents don't fit that model
very well, especially if they're
intended to discover and connect to new
MCP servers on the fly. RFC 7591 lets
the client register itself
programmatically. So in other words,
instead of depending on a human admin
that has to pre-wire every single future
connection, the agent can then say,
"Here's my metadata, here are my keys,
please issue me a client identity so
that I can participate in this
ecosystem."
And then lastly, we get to RFC 8693,
which is token exchange. So this answers
the question, I already have a token
from an earlier part of the chain, but
now I need a different token for the
next hop. How do I do that correctly?
This is the delegation primitive. It
allows one token to be traded for
another token with a different audience,
narrower scope, or explicit delegation
semantics. This is the RFC that matters
most once the agent actually begins
acting across systems on behalf of a
user. It is exactly what makes the
four-legged identity model possible
without just reusing the wrong token
everywhere.
So the cleanest way to think about this
whole slide is as a journey. First with
9728 the resource says here's the O
world that I belong to and then with
8414 the authorization server says
here's how to interact with me. Then
with 7591, the client says, "I need to
become a recognized participant." And
then finally with 8693, the system says,
"Now that you're in the chain, here's
how you can pass your identity forward."
So that sequence is exactly why these
four RFC's belong together. There are
not four unrelated standards. There are
four parts of one life cycle.
Discovering the resource, discovering
the O server, registering the client,
and then exchanging tokens as delegation
expands. And that's why MCP effectively
needs all four. Once agents are
operating dynamically instead of through
static manually provisioned
integrations, you need standards for
discovery, trust bootstrapping,
registration, and delegation. Otherwise,
you end up substituting brittle manual
config and overprivileged shortcuts for
a real identity architecture.
So now that we've talked through what
each of these RFC's does individually, I
want to show you what this actually
looks like in a real system. So this
slide shows the full life cycle, what
you can call the zero to token journey
of an agent interacting with an MCP
server for the first time. So imagine an
agent encountering a brand new MCP
server it has never seen before. So the
very first thing it does is use RFC
9728, which was resource metadata. So it
queries the MCP server and asks
essentially what are you and how do I
authenticate to you. The MCP server
responds with information about which
authorization server is it trusts and
what scopes are required. So once the
agent has that it moves to RFC 8414
which is authorization server metadata.
Now it knows which IDP or authorization
server to talk to and it fetches the
configuration. So it now knows where to
get tokens, where to send requests, and
what endpoints exist. So at this point,
the agent may also realize that it does
not actually have a registered identity
with that authorization server. So it
uses RFC 7591, which is dynamic client
registration. So it registers itself,
provides its metadata and keys and gets
back a client ID so it can participate
in the OOTH flow. Then it runs a normal
OOTH flow to obtain an access token. And
finally, once it needs to call
downstream APIs on behalf of the user,
it'll use RFC 8693, which is token
exchange. So this helps it transform
that token into one that is scoped
correctly for it for its next hop. So if
you zoom out a bit, what's happening
here is that identity is not just a
single static object anymore. It's
something that's discovered,
established, and then transformed step
by step as your agent moves through the
system. And that's the key shift from
traditional systems. Identity is now
becoming a process, not just a token.
So this slide is essentially your cheat
sheet or your mental model for when each
of these pieces applies. Instead of
thinking about RFC's as abstract
standards, you can think about them as
triggers in a system. If an agent
encounters a new system and doesn't have
a client identity yet, it needs to use
7591 to register. If it doesn't know how
to authenticate, it needs to use 8414 in
order to discover the authorization
server. If it's trying to call another
service while carrying user context,
that's 8693. It needs to exchange its
tokens. And if it doesn't know which O
system to use or what scopes are
required, that's 9728. It needs to ask
the resource itself. So instead of
memorizing these as standards, you can
map them directly to system behavior.
Each one corresponds to a very concrete
situation that arises in dynamic agent
workflows. And the reason this matters
is that in MCP all of these situations
and scenarios happen very frequently.
They don't just happen once at setup
time, but they happen continuously as
agents discover and interact with new
tools.
So now that we've talked about identity
and delegation, we'll need to zoom out
and ask what does this actually look
like in a production system? Because
while getting identity right is
necessary, it's not sufficient. You need
to enforce security at every single
layer. This is why I'm going to
introduce a few enterprise security
principles that you should implement. So
the first this slide starts with least
privilege, which is probably one of the
most important principles. An agent
should never operate with broad service
level credentials. They should always
act on behalf of a user with tightly
scoped permissions. So that means using
three-legged OOTH wherever possible,
issuing short-lived tokens, and
enforcing scopes at every single
boundary, not just once, but repeatedly
as requests are moving through the
system. A key detail here is that
validation doesn't just happen at the
gateway. It should also happen at every
single MCP server. So this means that
you don't just trust upstream systems
blindly. You revalidate identity at
every single hop. So the second one is
encryption. In an agentic system, data
is constantly moving between agents, MCP
servers, and APIs. And you need to
ensure that data is encrypted both at
rest and in transit, and that keys are
managed properly. So, envelope
encryption is especially important here.
Data encryption keys are generated and
used transiently, while key encryption
keys are stored securely in a vault.
This ensures that even if part of the
system is compromised, the blast radius
is still relatively limited. So at this
stage we're moving from identity as a
protocol problem to identity as part of
a broader security architecture.
So the next two principles are
observability and availability. In
agentic systems, observability is not
optional. It's very critical. Every
single tool invocation should be logged
with full context such as who initiated
it, which agent executed it, which tool
was called, what inputs were used, and
what that outcome was. Without that, you
lose the ability to debug, audit, or
even trust the system at all. And one
particularly important addition here is
DLP, which stands for data loss
prevention. Every outbound response
should be scanned for sensitive
information like PII or secrets. Because
agents can aggregate and transform data
in unexpected ways, you need safeguards
against accidental leakage. Tracing is
also key here. You want end-to-end
visibility across the entire chain from
the user to the agent to the MCP to the
API so that you can also understand how
those decisions are propagating. On the
availability side, these systems are now
infrastructure. That means you need to
think about scaling, failover, and
resilience. Kubernetes patterns like
rolling updates, autoscaling, and
circuit breakers become essential
because a failure in one part of the
chain can cascade very quickly if it's
not properly contained.
So the final principles are off
hardening and secret management. So this
is where you help close the gap that
attackers will typically target. Pike
Pixie
should be required for all flows to
prevent interception attacks. JWTs
should be validated not just once but at
multiple layers both at the gateway and
at the MCP server. The odd claim should
be enforced strictly so that tokens
cannot be reused across services.
Internal communication between services
should use MTLS ensuring that even
within your infrastructure identity is
always verified. And then lastly,
there's secret management. So one of the
biggest risks in these systems is
accidental exposure of credentials. So
the goal is to eliminate plain text
secrets entirely. Everything should be
managed through a vault, accessed via
roles and audited. Access should be just
in time, time limited, and automatically
revoked. Secrets should never be
hard-coded, never stored in source
control, and ideally rotated very
frequently. So by this point, what we've
built is not just an identity system,
but a layered security model that
assumes every part of the system could
fail and still helps to contain the
damage.
So stepping back a little bit, what are
some of the key takeaways that you
should take from all of this? So first
is that the four-legged identity problem
is not something that you can just
ignore. It's not an edge case anymore
and it's becoming the default now that
agents are getting involved. Second,
standard OOTH is not broken, but it is
incomplete. You are going to need
additional mechanisms like token
exchange to make multihop delegation
work correctly.
Third, broker patterns are often very
necessary in practice because IDP
support is very inconsistent.
Centralizing token exchange, caching,
and policy enforcement is how you turn
this into a scalable solution.
And finally, security is layered.
Identity alone is no longer enough. You
need validation, encryption,
observability, and strict secret
management all working together. If any
one of those layers is missing, the
system becomes vulnerable. So everything
we've talked about so far seems quite
abstract. RFC's, delegation chains, and
token transformations. So what I want to
do next is to help make this all very
concrete. So we've developed a few labs
that help demonstrate what this actually
looks like in practice.
So the first lab shows a very standard
token exchange flow. You have a user
logging in through a web application,
obtaining a token, and then exchanging
that token for a new one that is valid
for a downstream resource. What's useful
here is that you can actually see the
transformation. You can inspect the
token before and after the exchange and
see how the audience changes, how scopes
are adjusted, and how identity is
preserved. This is perhaps the simplest
working example of the concepts that
we've been discussing.
So the second lab helps to take this a
step further. Instead of having each
component handle token exchange
individually, you introduce a broker
layer. So this broker centralizes token
exchange, caching, and secret
management. It sits between the
application, the MCP server and
downstream APIs and it ensures the
identity is handled consistently. You
can see in the diagram that it
integrates with systems like keycloak
for identity, open bow for secrets and a
cache layer for token reuse. This is
much closer to what actual productive
production systems look like because
once you scale beyond a few services,
you're going to need a central central
place to help manage identity
transformations.
So, if you'd like to look at these labs
or try them out yourself, uh, feel free
to scan the QR code or go go to the link
on these slides and run through it
yourself. Yeah. Thank you guys so much
for listening. Um, I'm happy to answer
any questions that you guys have
afterwards.
